lessons.title: Variables are labeled boxes
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Make your page think

HTML builds the page and CSS paints it. **JavaScript** makes it *do* things: count points, react to clicks, change what's on screen.

JavaScript lives in its own file, `script.js`. The page loads it with a `<script>` tag at the very end of the `<body>`:

```html
<script src="script.js"></script>
```

### Variables are labeled boxes

A **variable** is a box with a label on it. You put a value in the box and use the label to find it later.

```js
let score = 0;
```

- `let` means "make a new box".
- `score` is the label.
- `=` puts the value `0` into the box.

To change what's inside, use the label again **without** `let`:

```js
score = score + 10; // now score is 10
```

If a box should **never** change, make it with `const` instead of `let`:

```js
const playerName = "Mia";
```

### Kinds of values

- **Numbers**: `7`, `3.5`, `-2` (no quotes)
- **Strings** (text): `"hello"` or `'hello'` (always in quotes)
- **Booleans**: just `true` or `false`

You can do math with `+ - * /`, and glue strings together with `+`:

```js
const name = "Mia";
console.log(name + " scored " + score); // Mia scored 10
```

### Seeing your results

`console.log(...)` prints something to the **Console**, a message box under the preview. Programmers use it all the time to check what their code is doing.

Everything after `//` on a line is a **comment**: a note for humans that JavaScript skips.

### New words

- **JavaScript**: the programming language that makes web pages interactive.
- **Variable**: a labeled box that holds a value.
- **Value**: the thing stored in a variable, like `10` or `"Mia"`.
- **String**: text inside quotes.
- **Boolean**: a value that's either `true` or `false`.
- **Console**: the message area where `console.log` prints.
- **Comment**: a note after `//` that the computer ignores.

lessons.title: Variables, values and types
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## JavaScript fundamentals

**JavaScript** (JS) is the programming language built into every browser. HTML gives a page structure and CSS gives it style. JS gives it **behavior**.

Load a script at the end of `<body>` so the elements above it already exist when it runs (you'll also see `<script src="script.js" defer>` in the `<head>`, which does the same thing):

```html
  <script src="script.js"></script>
</body>
```

### Declaring variables

```js
const maxLives = 3;   // can't be reassigned
let lives = maxLives; // can be reassigned
lives = lives - 1;
```

Default to **`const`**. Switch to `let` only when you need to reassign. You'll see `var` in older code. It has confusing scoping rules, so avoid it.

Names are **case-sensitive**, can't start with a digit, and by convention use **camelCase**: `highScore`, `isGameOver`.

### Types

Every value has a **type**. The **primitive** types you'll use most:

| Type | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| `number` | `42`, `3.14`, `-7` (integers and decimals are the same type) |
| `string` | `"hi"`, `'hi'`, `` `hi` `` |
| `boolean` | `true`, `false` |
| `undefined` | a variable that was declared but never given a value |
| `null` | "intentionally empty" |

`typeof` tells you the type: `typeof 42` is `"number"`.

### Template literals

Backtick strings can drop values in with `${...}`. That's much easier to read than gluing with `+`:

```js
const player = "Nova";
console.log(`${player} has ${lives} lives left`);
```

### Type coercion: a classic bug

With `+`, if **either** side is a string, JS joins instead of adding:

```js
"5" + 3        // "53"  (a string!)
Number("5") + 3 // 8
```

Values read from text boxes and URLs are always strings, so convert them with `Number()` before doing math.

### New words

- **Declaration**: creating a variable with `const` or `let`.
- **Primitive**: a basic value type: number, string, boolean, undefined, null (plus bigint and symbol).
- **camelCase**: joining words with each new word capitalized, like `highScore`.
- **Template literal**: a backtick string that can contain `${expressions}`.
- **Type coercion**: JS automatically converting a value from one type to another.

lessons.title: Comparisons and if/else
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Conditional logic

### Comparison operators

`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` compare. For equality, always use the **strict** operators `===` and `!==`. The loose `==` performs type coercion first, which causes surprises:

```js
5 == "5"   // true  (the string is converted)
5 === "5"  // false (different types)
0 == ""    // true  (!)
```

### Logical operators

| Operator | Name | True when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a && b` | AND | both are true |
| `a \|\| b` | OR | at least one is true |
| `!a` | NOT | `a` is false |

```js
const canEnter = age >= 13 && hasPermission;
```

### Truthy and falsy

`if` doesn't strictly need a boolean. These values are **falsy** (treated as false): `false`, `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Everything else is **truthy**, including `"0"`, `[]` and `{}`.

```js
const nickname = "";
if (!nickname) console.log("Please pick a nickname");
```

### if / else if / else

Branches are checked **top to bottom** and the **first** true one wins, so order matters:

```js
if (score >= 90) {
  grade = "A";
} else if (score >= 80) { // only reached if score < 90
  grade = "B";
} else {
  grade = "C or below";
}
```

### The ternary operator

For a simple either/or *value*, there's a one-line form: `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`.

```js
const label = lives > 0 ? "Playing" : "Game over";
```

### New words

- **Strict equality** (`===`): equal value **and** equal type, with no conversion.
- **Logical operator**: `&&`, `||` or `!`, used to combine or flip booleans.
- **Truthy / falsy**: whether a non-boolean value counts as true or false in a condition.
- **Ternary operator**: `condition ? a : b`, an inline if/else that produces a value.

lessons.title: Repeat it with loops
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Don't repeat yourself, loop!

Want to print the numbers 1 to 100? You *could* write 100 lines... or one **loop**. A loop runs the same code again and again.

### The for loop

```js
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  console.log(i);
}
// prints 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
```

The round brackets hold three parts, separated by `;`:

1. **Start**: `let i = 1` makes a counter called `i`.
2. **Keep going while**: `i <= 5`. The loop keeps running while this is `true`.
3. **Step**: `i++` adds 1 to `i` after each lap. (`i--` takes 1 away.)

Each time through the loop is called an **iteration**.

### Building something up

Loops often add to a variable a little at a time:

```js
let stars = "";
for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
  stars = stars + "⭐";
}
console.log(stars); // ⭐⭐⭐
```

### Careful: infinite loops

If the "keep going" part never becomes `false`, the loop never stops. That's an **infinite loop**. Codegrove stops yours after a moment and tells you, but on a real page it would freeze the tab!

### New words

- **Loop**: code that repeats.
- **Iteration**: one trip through the loop.
- **Counter**: a variable like `i` that keeps track of which lap you're on.
- **Infinite loop**: a loop that never stops because its condition never becomes false.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Iteration

### for

The workhorse. Initializer, condition, update:

```js
for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { /* runs with i = 0..4 */ }
```

Starting at `0` and using `<` is the convention, because arrays (next lessons) are numbered from 0. Being one step too many or too few is an **off-by-one error**, one of the most common bugs in programming. When a loop misbehaves, check `<` vs `<=` and the start value first.

### while and do…while

Use `while` when you don't know in advance how many iterations you need:

```js
let roll = 0;
let attempts = 0;
while (roll !== 6) {
  roll = Math.ceil(Math.random() * 6);
  attempts++;
}
```

`do { … } while (cond)` checks the condition **after** the body, so it always runs at least once.

### for…of

Loops over the items of anything **iterable**: strings (character by character), arrays, and more.

```js
for (const letter of "hey") {
  console.log(letter); // h, e, y
}
```

### break and continue

- `break` exits the loop immediately.
- `continue` skips the rest of this iteration and moves on to the next.

### The accumulator pattern

Declare a variable before the loop and update it inside: a running total, a count, a built-up string. You'll use this constantly.

```js
let total = 0;
for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) total += i; // += is shorthand for total = total + i
```

`%` (**remainder**, or *modulo*) is handy in loops: `n % 3 === 0` means `n` divides evenly by 3.

Codegrove's preview stops any loop that runs for more than 1.5 seconds, so an infinite loop shows an error instead of freezing your tab.

### New words

- **Iterable**: something you can loop over with `for…of`, like a string or array.
- **Off-by-one error**: a loop that runs one time too many or too few.
- **Accumulator**: a variable that collects a result across iterations.
- **Modulo** (`%`): the remainder after division. `7 % 3` is `1`.

lessons.title: Functions are recipes
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Write it once, use it lots

A **function** is like a recipe: a set of steps with a name. Write the recipe once, then use it whenever you want.

### Making a function

```js
function makeSandwich(filling) {
  return "Bread + " + filling + " + bread";
}
```

- `function` says "here comes a recipe".
- `makeSandwich` is its name.
- `filling` is a **parameter**: an ingredient the recipe needs. It goes in the round brackets.
- `return` hands the finished result back.

### Using a function

Using a function is called **calling** it. Write its name with round brackets, and put the ingredient inside:

```js
const lunch = makeSandwich("cheese");
console.log(lunch); // Bread + cheese + bread

console.log(makeSandwich("jam")); // Bread + jam + bread
```

The value you pass in (`"cheese"`) is called an **argument**. The same recipe works with any filling!

A function can have more than one parameter. Separate them with commas: `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }`

### New words

- **Function**: a named set of steps you can run again and again.
- **Parameter**: a name for an input the function needs, like `filling`.
- **Argument**: the actual value you give it when you call it, like `"cheese"`.
- **Return**: hand a result back to whoever called the function.
- **Call**: run a function by writing its name and `( )`.

lessons.title: Lists with arrays
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Keep lots of things in one place

A variable holds **one** value. An **array** holds a whole **list** of values, in order, inside square brackets:

```js
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
```

### Getting things out

Every item has a position number called its **index**. Computers start counting at **0**:

```js
fruits[0] // "apple"   (the first item!)
fruits[1] // "banana"
fruits[2] // "cherry"
```

`fruits.length` tells you how many items there are: `3`.

### Adding things

`push` adds an item to the **end** of the list:

```js
fruits.push("mango");
// ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "mango"]
```

You can `push` onto a `const` array. `const` stops you from swapping in a *different* list, but you can still change what's inside this one.

### Going through every item

A `for…of` loop visits each item, one at a time:

```js
for (const fruit of fruits) {
  console.log("I like " + fruit);
}
```

### New words

- **Array**: a list of values inside `[ ]`, kept in order.
- **Item**: one value in an array (also called an *element*).
- **Index**: an item's position number. The first one is `0`.
- **length**: how many items an array has.
- **push**: add an item to the end of an array.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Arrays

An **array** is an ordered list. Items are accessed by zero-based **index**; `arr.length` is the count and `arr[arr.length - 1]` is the last item (or use `arr.at(-1)`).

### Mutating methods

These change the original array:

| Method | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `push(x)` / `pop()` | add / remove at the end |
| `unshift(x)` / `shift()` | add / remove at the start |
| `splice(i, n)` | remove `n` items starting at index `i` |
| `sort()` | sort in place |

### Non-mutating methods

These return something new and leave the original alone:

| Method | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `includes(x)` | `true`/`false` |
| `indexOf(x)` | the index, or `-1` |
| `slice(start, end)` | a copy of part of the array |
| `map(fn)` | a new array of `fn(item)` for each item |
| `filter(fn)` | a new array of the items where `fn(item)` is truthy |
| `find(fn)` | the first item where `fn(item)` is truthy |
| `reduce(fn, start)` | one combined value |

`map`, `filter`, `find` and `reduce` take a **callback**: a function you pass in, which they call for each item. Arrow functions keep that short:

```js
const prices = [4, 12, 7];
const withTax = prices.map((p) => p * 1.1);
const cheap = prices.filter((p) => p < 10);       // [4, 7]
const total = prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0); // 23
```

`reduce` walks the array carrying an **accumulator** (`sum`), starting from the second argument (`0`).

### The sort trap

`sort()` with no callback compares items **as strings**: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives `[1, 10, 9]`. For numbers pass a comparator: `(a, b) => a - b` for ascending, `(a, b) => b - a` for descending. And `sort` mutates. To sort a copy, spread first:

```js
const sorted = [...scores].sort((a, b) => b - a);
```

The **spread** syntax `...` unpacks an array's items into a new array (or into a function call's arguments).

### New words

- **Mutate**: change the original value in place.
- **Callback**: a function passed to another function to be called later.
- **Comparator**: a callback telling `sort` how to order two items.
- **Spread** (`...`): unpacks an array's items, e.g. into a new array.

lessons.title: Objects describe things
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## One thing, lots of facts

An array is a list. An **object** describes *one thing* with labeled facts, inside curly braces `{ }`:

```js
const dog = {
  name: "Rex",
  breed: "beagle",
  age: 4,
};
```

Each fact is a **property**: a **key** (the label, like `name`), a colon, and a value (like `"Rex"`). Properties are separated by commas.

### Reading and changing properties

Use a dot:

```js
console.log(dog.name); // Rex

dog.age = dog.age + 1;   // happy birthday!
dog.tricks = "roll over"; // add a brand-new property
```

### Objects inside arrays

Lots of things, each described by an object? Put the objects in an array:

```js
const pets = [
  { name: "Rex", age: 4 },
  { name: "Mittens", age: 2 },
];
console.log(pets[1].name); // Mittens
```

### New words

- **Object**: a group of labeled facts about one thing, inside `{ }`.
- **Property**: one labeled fact in an object, like `age: 4`.
- **Key**: the label of a property, like `age`.
- **Dot notation**: reading or changing a property with a dot, like `dog.age`.

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Objects

An **object** groups related data (and behavior) under named keys.

```js
const book = {
  title: "Hatchet",
  author: "Gary Paulsen",
  pages: 195,
  tags: ["survival", "adventure"],
  publisher: { name: "Bradbury", year: 1987 }, // nested object
};
```

### Dot vs bracket notation

```js
book.title           // dot: when you know the key while writing the code
book["title"]        // bracket: same thing
const field = "pages";
book[field]          // bracket: when the key is in a variable
book.publisher.year  // nested access
book.isbn            // a missing key gives undefined (not an error)
```

### Methods and this

A function stored on an object is a **method**. Inside a method written with `function` or the shorthand syntax, `this` refers to the object it was called on:

```js
const counter = {
  count: 0,
  increment() {
    this.count++;
    return this.count;
  },
};
counter.increment(); // 1
```

(Arrow functions don't get their own `this`, so don't use them for methods that need it.)

### Looping over objects

`Object.keys(obj)`, `Object.values(obj)` and `Object.entries(obj)` return arrays you can loop over or `reduce`.

### Destructuring

Pull properties out into variables in one line:

```js
const { title, pages } = book; // same as const title = book.title; …
```

### References: copying isn't automatic

Objects (and arrays) are stored by **reference**. Assigning one to another variable does **not** copy it:

```js
const a = { hp: 10 };
const b = a;      // b points at the SAME object
b.hp = 0;
console.log(a.hp); // 0 !
```

To copy, spread into a new object. Later properties win, so you can copy and change in one step:

```js
const boosted = { ...a, hp: 99 }; // a is untouched
```

That's a **shallow** copy: nested objects inside are still shared.

### New words

- **Method**: a function stored as a property of an object.
- **this**: inside a method, the object the method was called on.
- **Destructuring**: unpacking properties into variables, like `const { a, b } = obj`.
- **Reference**: a pointer to an object; two variables can point at the same one.
- **Shallow copy**: a new outer object whose nested objects are still shared.

lessons.title: Change the page with the DOM
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## JavaScript meets your page

So far your code has talked to the Console. Now it's going to change the **page itself**!

When the browser reads your HTML, it builds a family tree of every element on the page. That tree is called the **DOM** (*Document Object Model*). JavaScript can find any element in the tree and change it.

### Find an element

`document.querySelector` finds the first element that matches a CSS selector, just like in your style sheets:

```js
const title = document.querySelector("#title"); // the element with id="title"
```

### Change its text and style

```js
title.textContent = "Welcome!";  // change the words inside
title.style.color = "teal";      // change a style
title.style.fontSize = "40px";   // CSS's font-size becomes fontSize
```

### Add a brand-new element

Three steps: create it, fill it in, add it to the page.

```js
const item = document.createElement("li"); // 1. create
item.textContent = "Pancakes";             // 2. fill in
document.querySelector("ul").append(item); // 3. add it inside the <ul>
```

That's why the `<script>` tag goes at the **end** of the body: the elements have to exist before JavaScript can find them.

### New words

- **DOM** (*Document Object Model*): the browser's tree of everything on the page, which JavaScript can read and change.
- **querySelector**: finds the first element that matches a CSS selector.
- **textContent**: the text inside an element.
- **createElement**: makes a new element (it isn't on the page until you `append` it).
- **append**: puts an element inside another one, at the end.

lessons.title: Events
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Events

Interactive pages are **event-driven**: your code registers listeners, then waits for the browser to report what happened.

```js
button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log(event.target); // the element that was actually clicked
});
```

### The event object

Every listener receives an **event object** describing what happened:

| Property / method | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `event.target` | the element where the event started |
| `event.currentTarget` | the element the listener is attached to |
| `event.key` | for keyboard events: which key, e.g. `"Enter"` |
| `event.preventDefault()` | cancel the browser's default action |

### Common events

`click`, `input` (fires on every change to a text field), `change`, `submit` (on a `<form>`), `keydown`, `focus`/`blur`.

### Forms: listen for submit, not click

Listen for `submit` on the **form**. It fires for a button click *and* for pressing Enter in a field, which also makes it more accessible. A form's default action is to send the data and load a new page, so call `preventDefault()` to stay put:

```js
form.addEventListener("submit", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const value = input.value.trim(); // trim removes spaces at both ends
  if (!value) return;               // ignore empty input
  // …use value…
});
```

### Bubbling and event delegation

Events **bubble**: after firing on the target, they travel up through each parent element. So one listener on a parent can handle events from all its children, **including children added later**. That's **event delegation**:

```js
list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest("button.delete"); // the delete button that was clicked, if any
  if (!button) return;                                   // the click was somewhere else
  button.closest("li").remove();
});
```

`closest(selector)` walks up from an element to the nearest ancestor (or itself) that matches. Delegation means fewer listeners and nothing to re-attach when the list changes.

### New words

- **Event-driven**: code that runs in response to events rather than top-to-bottom once.
- **Event object**: the argument a listener receives, describing the event.
- **Default action**: what the browser does on its own, like submitting a form.
- **Bubbling**: an event travelling up from its target through the parent elements.
- **Event delegation**: one listener on a parent handling events for many children.

lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Ask a server for data

Weather apps don't know the weather by themselves. They **ask a server** on the internet, and the server sends back data. A website made for programs (instead of people) to ask for data is called an **API** (*Application Programming Interface*).

### The answer looks like objects

APIs usually answer in **JSON** (*JavaScript Object Notation*). It looks almost exactly like the objects you already know:

```json
{ "town": "Maple Hollow", "tempC": 18 }
```

### Asking with fetch

`fetch` sends the request. The answer takes a moment to arrive, so we say what to do **then**:

```js
fetch("https://api.codegrove.test/weather")
  .then((response) => response.json()) // turn the answer into an object
  .then((data) => {
    console.log(data.town);            // use it!
  });
```

- `fetch(address)` asks the server.
- The first `.then` turns the reply into JavaScript data with `.json()`.
- The second `.then` gets that data, so this is where you put it on the page.

`(data) => { … }` is a short way to write a function. It works just like `function (data) { … }`.

### Codegrove's practice API

The preview can only talk to Codegrove's practice API, at `https://api.codegrove.test`. Try `/weather`, `/pets` or `/planets`. On a real website, the same code works with real APIs.

### New words

- **API** (*Application Programming Interface*): a way for programs to ask another program, often a server, for data.
- **JSON** (*JavaScript Object Notation*): a text format for data that looks like JavaScript objects.
- **fetch**: the JavaScript command that asks a server for something.
- **Server**: a computer that answers requests over the internet.

lessons.title: fetch, JSON and APIs
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Talking to APIs

An **API** (*Application Programming Interface*) is a contract for how programs talk to each other. On the web that usually means a server exposing **endpoints**, URLs like `/planets/3`, that you call over **HTTP** (*HyperText Transfer Protocol*) and that answer with **JSON** (*JavaScript Object Notation*).

### HTTP in one table

| Piece | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Method** | `GET` (read), `POST` (create), `PUT`/`PATCH` (update), `DELETE` |
| **Status code** | `200` OK, `201` Created, `400` Bad Request, `404` Not Found, `500` Server Error |
| **Body** | the data, usually JSON |

### JSON

JSON is a text format based on JS object syntax, but stricter: keys and strings need **double quotes**, there are no functions, `undefined` or comments, and no trailing commas.

```js
JSON.stringify({ id: 3, name: "Earth" }); // '{"id":3,"name":"Earth"}'
JSON.parse('{"id":3}').id;                  // 3
```

### Promises and async/await

Network requests take time, so `fetch` returns a **Promise**: a placeholder for a value that arrives later. You can chain `.then()`, but `async`/`await` reads top to bottom:

```js
async function loadPlanet(id) {
  const response = await fetch(`https://api.codegrove.test/planets/${id}`);
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  }
  return await response.json();
}
```

`await` pauses *this function* (not the whole page) until the Promise settles. It only works inside an `async` function, and an `async` function always returns a Promise.

### The trap: fetch doesn't fail on 404

`fetch` only **rejects** (throws) when the request can't happen at all, e.g. you're offline. A `404` or `500` is still a successful *delivery* of a response. Always check `response.ok` (true for 200–299) or `response.status` yourself.

### Handling errors

Wrap awaited calls in `try…catch`, and always show the user *something*: a loading message first, then the data or a friendly error.

```js
try {
  const planet = await loadPlanet(3);
  status.textContent = planet.name;
} catch (error) {
  status.textContent = "Couldn't load the planet. Try again later.";
}
```

### The practice API

The preview has no internet access, so Codegrove provides a practice API at `https://api.codegrove.test` (`.test` addresses are reserved, so they never point at a real site):

| Endpoint | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /planets` | all 8 planets: `{ id, name, moons, hasRings, type }` |
| `GET /planets/:id` | one planet, or `404` with `{ error }` |
| `GET /pets` | shelter pets: `{ id, name, species, age, adopted }` |
| `GET /weather` | `{ town, tempC, conditions, windKph }` |

### New words

- **Endpoint**: one URL an API answers on, like `/planets/3`.
- **HTTP** (*HyperText Transfer Protocol*): the rules browsers and servers use to send requests and responses.
- **Status code**: the 3-digit number that says how a request went.
- **JSON** (*JavaScript Object Notation*): the text format APIs use to send data.
- **Promise**: an object representing a value that will be ready later.
- **async / await**: syntax for writing Promise-based code that reads top to bottom.
